title: AI Leaders Are Refineries, Not Native-App Winners
dek: AI enters the agent era: first-phase leaders are just refineries, not native-app winners; new platforms don't come from old platforms; organizations shift from roles to tasks; ultimately, humans compete on creativity that creates something from nothing.
why: Zeng Ming offers a three-phase industrial history framework to give you a coordinate system for locating AI's current position—a cure for the optimism of "this time it's different"—while also revealing the window of opportunity for application entrepreneurs and the brutal expectations for giants in transition.
who: CEOs making AI strategy, executives at traditional giants seeking a second curve, AI investors, and tech founders torn between building models or applications.
skip: The rapid-fire Q&A and book list at the end can be skipped (after 2:29).

points.h: Building agents today is like building websites in 1992
points.body: Zeng Ming divides the industrialization of general-purpose technologies into three phases: first, becoming social infrastructure; second, an explosion of applications; and finally, the emergence of native applications. The consensus forming around tokens as a unit of measurement in 2026 signals the maturity of the first phase; the agent events around the Spring Festival (colloquially called "lobster") mark AI's official entry into the agent era. He compares this to the website-building movement of 1992: back then people built websites to share information; today they build agents to share capabilities. The browser hasn't appeared yet; whoever can establish agent standards and seize the user entry point may be the biggest opportunity in the next two years.

points.h: A ten-trillion-dollar company will emerge, but not these two
points.body: Zeng Ming states outright that OpenAI and Anthropic are remarkable technical and commercial achievements, but business history shows that the companies that break out in the first wave are likely not the big winners of the native-application phase. Yahoo was worth $120 billion five years after its founding, and AOL reached a valuation of $220 billion, yet neither became the Google of the next era. Model companies are more like AI cloud companies—refineries that extract base oil—while the real application value belongs to chemical plants and car companies, and cars were not built by oil companies. He believes a ten-trillion-dollar company will certainly emerge, but it may not be either of the current leaders. Model companies will trend toward an oligopoly with heavy government regulation—a mature business.

points.h: The unit of AI-native organizations is tasks, not roles
points.body: Corporations correspond to the industrial-era bureaucracy; AI disrupts the industrial era, and the corporate system will decline. The basic unit of an AI-native organization is not a role but a task: people are not organized by reporting lines but flow around "what problem needs solving," with humans and AI collaborating around tasks. Consequently, well-designed positions and hierarchies will disappear, and traditional middle management will die out. Future founders must first define their organization's task network. Silicon Valley's New Lab is a prototype of the new organizational form, and OpenAI itself resembles a Lab more than a traditional company. The culture of new organizations is more like a sports team, emphasizing transparency, sharing, and co-creation, rather than relying on commands and assessments.

points.h: Excellence is judged only in hindsight; being good is visible on the spot
points.body: Zeng Ming argues that "being good is not the same as being excellent." Being good is growth sustained by positive feedback, while excellence requires overcoming repeated negative feedback, persisting when everyone disapproves, and ultimately proving oneself a prophet of the era through enormous success—so "excellence is judged only in hindsight." Those who are merely good easily fall into a cycle of proving themselves, leading to conservative strategies. Excellent people have a small ego, tend to attribute success to the era and their partners, and are driven by mission rather than external valuation. When identifying founders, he asks, "What kind of self would you be satisfied with in ten years?" If the answer is "a company worth ten billion dollars," that is mainly ego-driven, not an inner mission. Truly excellent founders are often altruistic and empathetic.

points.h: Strategy in the AI era cannot be planned; it must be generated
points.body: In the AI era, strategy is not planning but generation. Zeng Ming proposes a "strategy generation system": organizations must build an environment and network that allows strategic insights to emerge naturally. Because decision frequency is higher and quality demands are greater, CEOs cannot rely on linear extrapolation for planning, nor can they outsource strategy to McKinsey—McKinsey's rise was a product of the slow maturity of the industrial era. His methodology is "look ten years, think three years, act one year," with the core being "think three years": you must see at least two or three milestones ahead, creating tension between short-term actions and the medium-term vision. Organizational building must ensure sufficient context rather than control, enabling the right people to make the right decisions at the right time.

points.h: The right analogy for robots is appliances, not cars
points.body: Zeng Ming believes robotics is still in the strategic exploration phase, far from convergence. Currently, two routes—building a generalized brain first or closing the loop in specific scenarios first—are both logically valid, and it's impossible to know in advance which will be faster. Historically, the automobile industry had thousands of companies from 1900 to 1920, and it wasn't until Ford built the assembly line in 1913 that scaling began; robots have yet to see their Model T moment, and whoever truly sells ten thousand robots first would already be remarkable. But a better analogy for robots is appliances rather than cars: after electricity was invented, refrigerators, washing machines, air conditioners, and countless other categories emerged. Robots interacting with the physical world will have N major scenarios, and home, companionship, and industrial uses may each produce their own native giants.

points.h: Giants that feel safe are the least safe
points.body: Zeng Ming says that in the face of a tidal wave, no one is safe; feeling safe is the most unsafe. In business history, no company has ever transitioned smoothly from one era to the next; IBM and Microsoft are the only possible exceptions, and both are fraught with uncertainty. AI is a productivity revolution that disrupts the Industrial Revolution, not a continuation innovation like mobile internet, so the technological reserves and organizational culture of old giants are liabilities. Google can survive as an AI cloud company, but it may not capture the consumer entry point; ByteDance has an AI cloud opportunity, but Doubao is not the future application; Tencent's social relationships will be restructured; Alibaba is not naturally safe either. New platforms will likely be created by new companies.

points.h: Human value lies in creating something from nothing, not in writing songs or painting
points.body: Drawing on Drucker's framework, Zeng Ming defines the AI era as the age of creativity: any knowledge work that can be structured will be taken over by AI. Humans are both forced and finally liberated to develop new potential. This potential is creativity—not writing songs or painting, but the ability to originally define complex problems and create something from nothing. AI has already taken all existing knowledge; human value lies in creating what does not yet exist. Hence he calls his mission "being a happy researcher" and believes civilization's next step will reorganize around creativity, even forcing the education system to shift from "knowledge indoctrination" to "open exploration," because young people already know the old path leads nowhere.

terms.def: Treating AI compute as infrastructure that produces tokens, symbolizing intelligence entering a standardized, metered phase.
An operating system that can directly orchestrate all agents to complete tasks based on intent; Zeng Ming believes this belongs to the third phase and cannot be implemented yet.
A new organizational form dissatisfied with the corporate system, centered on researchers; OpenAI is seen as the earliest example.
A Silicon Valley buzzword meaning taking control of one's own destiny, proactively seeking tasks and growth, replacing hierarchical command-driven behavior.
A management philosophy: provide ample shared context and information so members can autonomously make correct decisions.

quotes.text: The most successful companies are always contrarian, but being contrarian does not guarantee success.
It may not survive to the end. It will likely do well later on, but it is probably not the big player, the big winner of the native-application phase.
Companies in the first phase find it hard to survive into the second phase, and companies in the second phase find it hard to survive into the third.

So companies will disappear; companies will die out. There's nothing to regret about that. In the future there will be more interesting things—how many people actually enjoy going to work at a company now? They don't.

My technology is so great, I've created so much value—why might my company not be worth much? Because of the basic laws of economics: as long as there is homogeneous supply, you cannot capture high profits; you are just a company that isn't worth much.

Excellence is judged only in hindsight, because you overcome negative feedback again and again, and when everyone disapproves of you, you finally prove through enormous success that you were the earliest prophet of the era.
I have always believed that in the face of a tidal wave, no one is safe; whoever feels safe is the most unsafe.
